blocks.body:
Java is one of the most widely used programming languages in the world. It was designed so you can write programs that run on a huge variety of devices — from smartphones to mainframe computers in a bank.

Java is "object-oriented". This means: you build your program out of small, reusable building blocks called "objects" — for example, an object could be a "car" or a "user account", each with its own properties (e.g. color, account balance) and abilities (e.g. drive, deposit money).

blocks.robotComment: This 'write once, run anywhere' thing is honestly one of my favorite superpowers. 🤖
blocks.body: A well-known motto of Java is: "Write once, run anywhere". This is possible because Java code isn't executed directly by the operating system, but by an intermediary program called the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). The JVM exists for Windows, macOS, Linux, and more — your code doesn't need to worry about that.

blocks.question: What does "Write once, run anywhere" mean for Java?
options: Thanks to the JVM, Java code runs on different operating systems without needing to be changed
You only ever have to write Java code once in your life
Java code only works on Windows
Java automatically translates the code into other languages like Python
blocks.explanation: "Write once, run anywhere" means: you write your Java code once, and thanks to the JVM it runs on every operating system without you needing to adapt it.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Ooh, a trick question — think carefully before you answer.

blocks.explanation: Java was developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (today Java belongs to Oracle) — not by Microsoft.

blocks.robotComment: Ever wonder where the name 'Java' actually came from? Let's find out. ☕
blocks.body: The history of Java begins in 1991 at Sun Microsystems. A team led by developer James Gosling was working on a language for small, smart devices like set-top boxes. At the time, the project wasn't yet called "Java" but "Oak" — named after a tree outside Gosling's office window.

blocks.question: What was Java called before it got its current name?
blocks.explanation: Java was originally called "Oak", named after a tree outside James Gosling's office.

blocks.robotComment: That coffee connection explains more than you would think. ☕
blocks.body: The name "Oak" was already trademarked, so in 1995 the team needed a new name. The developers drank a lot of coffee — and Java is the name of a well-known type of coffee (named after the Indonesian island of Java, where coffee is grown). That's how the language got its current name and its logo: a steaming cup of coffee.

blocks.sentence: Java was named after a type of ___.
blocks.explanation: The name "Java" comes from a type of coffee that is named after the Indonesian island of Java.

blocks.body: Java was officially released in 1995. Since then, the language has been constantly evolving: Java 8 (2014), for example, introduced a major new feature called "lambda expressions", which made writing code more concise. Since 2018, a new Java version has been released roughly every six months.

blocks.robotComment: See if you remember who's in charge of Java today. 🤔
blocks.body: In 2010, the company Oracle bought Sun Microsystems — since then, Oracle has owned and maintained the Java language.

blocks.statement: Oracle owns and maintains Java today.
blocks.explanation: Oracle acquired Sun Microsystems in 2010 and has been responsible for the ongoing development of Java ever since.

blocks.robotComment: Picking your first language is a big decision — here's why Java's a great one. 🎯
blocks.body: There are many programming languages — so why is it worth starting with Java specifically? That means huge demand for Java developers on the job market, whether at startups, banks, or big tech companies.

blocks.robotComment: Strictly typed sounds intimidating, but Java is really just looking out for you. 🛡️
blocks.body: Java also teaches you solid fundamentals that will help you with other languages too. Because Java has very clear, strict rules (this is called "strictly typed"), you get used to writing clean, structured code right from the start.

blocks.question: What is one important reason many people learn Java?

Java is the only language you can use to build websites
Java has no rules at all — you can write anything however you like

blocks.robotComment: Big community means you're never stuck for long. 🤝
blocks.body: Another advantage: Java has a huge, active community. That means for almost every problem, you can already find a solution online, a ready-made library, or someone who can help you.

blocks.robotComment: Banks trust Java because it just does not break. 🏦

blocks.explanation: Banks and other large companies rely on Java because it is stable and reliable for important enterprise software.

blocks.body: 🌐 Web backends: Using frameworks like Spring, many companies build the "server side" of their websites and apps in Java — the part that processes and stores data behind the scenes.

blocks.robotComment: From your phone to massive data centers — Java really gets around. 📊

blocks.robotComment: Source code is just text you write — Java turns it into something real. 📝
blocks.body: When you write a Java program, you type text into a file — for example Main.java. This human-readable text is called "source code". It consists of words and symbols that follow strict, well-defined rules, but is still readable to you.

code.caption: This is source code. You can read and understand it, even if you don't know every detail yet.

blocks.body: A computer, however, cannot execute this text directly. A processor only understands "machine language" — tiny electrical signals represented as zeros and ones. Source code is therefore an intermediate stage: understandable for humans, but not yet directly executable by the hardware.

blocks.robotComment: Think about what a processor actually understands before you answer. 🤔
blocks.statement: A computer processor can execute Java source code directly, without translating it first.
blocks.explanation: A processor only understands machine language. Java source code must first be translated before it can be executed.

blocks.body: Java source code is always saved in files with the extension ".java". The file name must match the name of the public class inside the file — so the file for our example above would need to be called "Main.java", because the class is named "Main".

blocks.sentence: Java source code files always have the file extension ___.
blocks.explanation: Source code files in Java always end in ".java" — for example "Main.java".

blocks.robotComment: You've got the starting point down — next up, how it becomes runnable. ➡️
blocks.body: In summary: source code is the starting point of every Java program. It is the text that you, as a developer, write, read, and edit yourself. Later — with the help of another tool — this text becomes something the computer can actually execute. You will learn about this tool in the next lesson.

blocks.question: What best describes "source code"?
options: The human-readable text that you write in a Java file (.java)
The zeros and ones that the processor understands directly
A program that installs other programs
A file that only contains images
blocks.explanation: Source code is the human-written and human-readable text of a program, stored in a .java file.

blocks.statement: The file name of a Java source code file must match the name of the public class it contains.
blocks.explanation: If a class is named "Main", the file must be named "Main.java" — the file name and the public class name must match.

blocks.robotComment: Your code needs a translator before the computer can run it — meet the compiler. 🔧
blocks.body: You now know that source code is human-readable, but the computer cannot execute it directly. This is exactly where the "compiler" comes in — a program that translates your source code.

The Java compiler is called "javac" (short for "Java Compiler"). It reads your .java file and translates it into a new file that the computer can process more easily. This process is called "compiling".

code.code: javac Main.java
code.caption: This is how you call the compiler on the command line: "javac" plus the name of your source code file.

blocks.sentence: The Java compiler is called ___.
blocks.explanation: "javac" is the command-line tool that compiles (translates) Java source code.

blocks.robotComment: Bytecode is the next big idea — we dig into it properly next lesson. 👀
blocks.body: Important: the compiler does not translate your code directly into machine language for a specific processor. Instead, it produces a special intermediate form called "bytecode" — more on that in the next lesson. This intermediate form is the trick that makes Java runnable on so many different devices.

The compiler also checks your code for errors. If, for example, you made a typo or forgot a bracket, the compiler stops with an error message and does not produce a translated file. This is called a "compile error".

blocks.question: What happens if your Java source code contains a typo?
options: The compiler stops with an error message and does not produce a translated file
The compiler ignores the error and just keeps going
blocks.explanation: If the compiler finds an error in the source code, it reports a compile error and does not produce a runnable translated file.

blocks.robotComment: That translator analogy is a good one to hold onto — think it through before you answer. 🕵️
blocks.body: You can think of the compiler like a translator converting a book from one language into another — except it also checks every sentence for grammar mistakes before translating it.

blocks.statement: The Java compiler translates source code directly into machine language for a specific processor.
blocks.explanation: The compiler translates source code into bytecode — a platform-independent intermediate form, not directly into machine language for a specific processor.

blocks.robotComment: Compiling does not produce a finished program yet — there is a step in between. 🔍
blocks.body: When the compiler ("javac") translates your source code, the result is not a finished file for Windows, macOS, or Linux — but "bytecode". Bytecode is an intermediate form: no longer human-readable text, but also not machine language for a specific processor.
Bytecode is saved in a new file with the extension ".class". So after compiling, "Main.java" becomes "Main.class".

code.code:
javac Main.java
// produces: Main.class
code.caption: The compiler reads Main.java and produces the bytecode file Main.class from it.

blocks.sentence: Bytecode files in Java have the file extension ___.
blocks.explanation: Compiled Java bytecode is stored in files with the extension ".class".

blocks.body: What is special about bytecode is that it is platform-independent. This means the same .class file can be used on a Windows PC, a Mac, or a Linux server — the bytecode itself is identical everywhere. No recompiling needed for each operating system!

blocks.statement: Bytecode is different for each operating system and must be freshly generated for Windows, macOS, and Linux.
blocks.explanation: Bytecode is platform-independent — the same .class file works on every operating system without being recompiled.

blocks.body: Bytecode still isn't what the processor directly understands, though. It is a kind of "intermediate language", made specifically to be read by another program — the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which you will learn about in the next lesson. It is exactly this combination of bytecode and JVM that makes Java's motto "Write once, run anywhere" possible.
blocks.robotComment: This combo is exactly what makes write once, run anywhere possible. 🌐

blocks.question: Why is bytecode so important for Java?
options: Because it is platform-independent and works on any operating system with a matching JVM
Because it is executed directly by the processor, without further help
Because it is easier for humans to read than source code
Because it completely replaces the .java file, which can then be deleted
blocks.explanation: Bytecode is platform-independent — it runs anywhere a JVM is available, without the code needing to be rewritten for every system.

blocks.robotComment: One more piece of the puzzle before the JVM takes center stage. ➡️
blocks.body: In summary: source code (.java) is translated by the compiler into bytecode (.class). Bytecode is not yet machine language, but a platform-independent intermediate form waiting to be executed.

blocks.statement: Bytecode is created when the compiler translates a .java file.
blocks.explanation: The compiler (javac) reads the .java source code file and produces a .class file containing bytecode from it.

blocks.robotComment: Bytecode needs someone to actually run it — say hello to the JVM. 👋
blocks.body: You have learned that the compiler produces bytecode (a .class file) from your source code. But who actually executes this bytecode? The answer: the "Java Virtual Machine", or JVM for short.

The JVM is a program that runs on your operating system and reads bytecode. It translates the bytecode step by step into the machine language that your specific device's processor understands — whether that's a Windows PC, a Mac, or a Linux server.

code.code: java Main
code.caption: This is how you start the JVM on the command line: "java" plus the name of the compiled class (without .class).

blocks.sentence: The JVM translates ___ into machine language for the respective processor.
blocks.explanation: The JVM takes the platform-independent bytecode (.class file) and translates it for the respective processor.

blocks.robotComment: Bytecode is universal, but is the JVM itself the same everywhere? Think before you answer. 🤔
blocks.body: Every operating system has its own matching version of the JVM. This is exactly why "Write once, run anywhere" works: you write your code once, compile it once into bytecode — and it can be executed anywhere a matching JVM is installed.

blocks.statement: Windows, macOS, and Linux each have different versions of the JVM.
blocks.explanation: Each operating system needs its own matching JVM version so that the same bytecode can be executed on it.

blocks.robotComment: Watch how these three pieces line up into one complete pipeline. 🔗
blocks.body: The complete process looks like this: you write Main.java (source code). The compiler javac translates it into Main.class (bytecode). The JVM reads Main.class and executes it by translating it into machine language for your device.

blocks.question: What is the main task of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM)?
options: It executes bytecode by translating it into machine language for the respective processor
It writes source code automatically for you
It stores Java files in the cloud
It translates machine language back into source code
blocks.explanation: The JVM reads bytecode and translates it for the processor of the respective device, so that the program actually runs.

blocks.robotComment: Without this piece, none of the bytecode magic would matter at all. 🔑
blocks.body: The JVM is thus the crucial link between platform-independent bytecode and the actual device your program is meant to run on. Without a JVM, no Java program could be executed.

blocks.statement: Without an installed JVM, a device cannot execute Java bytecode files.
blocks.explanation: The JVM is required to execute bytecode. Without it, a device cannot start compiled Java code.

blocks.robotComment: Time to find out where javac and the JVM actually come from. 📦
blocks.body: You now know three building blocks: source code, the compiler (javac), and the JVM. But where do you actually get these tools? The answer: you install the "Java Development Kit", or JDK for short.

The JDK is a complete package for developers. It contains everything you need to write and build Java programs: the compiler (javac), the JVM for testing your program, plus additional tools and libraries (ready-made code building blocks that others have already written).

code.code:
javac Main.java   // Part of the JDK: translates source code into bytecode
java Main          // Part of the JDK: executes the bytecode
code.caption: Both command-line tools, javac and java, are included in the JDK.

blocks.sentence: Anyone who wants to write and compile Java programs installs the ___.
blocks.explanation: The JDK (Java Development Kit) contains the compiler and all the tools needed to write and build Java programs.

blocks.robotComment: Think of it like a toolbox — everything you need is already inside. 🧰
blocks.body: You can think of the JDK like a complete workshop: it contains not just the machine that uses the finished workpiece (the JVM), but also all the tools needed to actually produce the workpiece in the first place (the compiler and more).

blocks.question: What is included in the JDK (Java Development Kit)?
options: The compiler (javac), the JVM, plus other developer tools and libraries
Only a text editor for writing notes
Only the JVM, but no compiler
Only a collection of images for Java logos
blocks.explanation: The JDK bundles the compiler, the JVM, and additional tools/libraries — everything developers need to build Java programs.

blocks.robotComment: Curious what happens if you skip the JDK entirely? Let us see. 🤔
blocks.body: Without the JDK you might still be able to run finished Java programs (often less is needed for that), but you cannot compile your own source code. So if you want to write your own Java programs, you need the JDK on your computer.

blocks.statement: You need the JDK to compile your own Java source code.
blocks.explanation: The compiler (javac), which is needed to compile source code, is part of the JDK.

blocks.body: In the next lesson you will learn about the JDK's counterpart: the JRE — designed for anyone who only wants to run Java programs, without developing them.

blocks.robotComment: Not everyone who runs Java wants to write it too. 🎬
blocks.body: Not everyone who uses Java wants to write their own code, too. Imagine you simply download a finished Java program to use it — for that, you don't need anything for compiling. That's what the "Java Runtime Environment", or JRE for short, is for.

The JRE contains the JVM along with the libraries needed to run Java programs — but no compiler. With the JRE you can execute finished bytecode (.class files), but you cannot compile your own source code.

code.code:
java Main   // works with the JRE — executes bytecode
javac Main.java   // does NOT work with the JRE alone — no compiler included
code.caption: The JRE is enough to run a program (java), but not to compile one (javac).

blocks.question: What is missing from the JRE (Java Runtime Environment) compared to the JDK?
blocks.explanation: The JRE contains the JVM and libraries for running programs, but no compiler — so compiling source code isn't possible with it.

blocks.robotComment: This analogy makes the JDK vs JRE split click instantly. 📀
blocks.body: You can think of the JRE like a DVD player: it can play finished movies, but it can't produce movies. The JDK, on the other hand, would be the entire film studio — including cameras, editing software, and the player to watch the final result.

blocks.statement: With the JRE alone, you can compile your own Java source code into bytecode.
blocks.explanation: The JRE does not contain a compiler. The JDK is needed to compile source code.

blocks.robotComment: One more distinction before we wrap up this whole pipeline. 🔗
blocks.body: So if you only want to use Java software (for example, to start a program), the JRE is enough. If you want to develop your own Java programs, you need the full JDK — the JRE is automatically included with it, since without the JVM you couldn't even test your program.

blocks.sentence: The ___ contains the JVM and the libraries for running Java programs, but no compiler.
blocks.explanation: The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is enough to run Java programs, but does not contain a compiler for translating source code.

blocks.body: In summary, you now know the whole pipeline: you write source code (.java). The compiler from the JDK translates it into bytecode (.class). The JVM — included in both the JDK and the JRE — executes this bytecode. Developers install the JDK; people who just use Java software often only need the JRE.

blocks.robotComment: Every Java program needs a home for its code — that's exactly what a class gives it. 🏠
blocks.body: In Java, every piece of code you write lives inside a class. A class is like a container or blueprint that holds all your program code together. Without a class, there is no program in Java.

code.code:
public class Main {

}
code.caption: The keyword "class" followed by the name of the class — here the class is called "Main".

blocks.robotComment: Notice how 'public' opens the door for other code to use this class. 🚪
blocks.body: The keyword "class" tells the Java compiler: "A new class starts here." Before it usually comes "public" — this means the class is visible and usable from anywhere, not just within its own file.

code.code:
public class Car {

}
code.caption: This is also a valid (still empty) class — it's simply called "Car" instead of "Main".

blocks.sentence: In Java, every piece of code you write belongs inside a ___.
blocks.explanation: All Java code lives inside a class. Methods are part of the code too, but they themselves are located inside a class.

blocks.robotComment: Capital letters for class names — small rule, big consistency win. 🔤
blocks.body: By convention, a class name should start with a capital letter, for example "Main", "Car", or "Calculator". This isn't a strict compiler rule, but practically every Java developer follows it so code looks consistent for everyone.

blocks.question: What best describes a class in Java?
options: A container or blueprint that holds your code together
A single number in the program
A comment that the compiler ignores
An error message from the compiler
blocks.explanation: A class is the container that holds all your Java code — comparable to a blueprint that ties everything together.

blocks.robotComment: Every Java program needs at least one of these to even exist. 🏗️
blocks.body: A Java program can't exist without at least one class — all the code must be housed inside one. Next, we'll look at how a program inside such a class actually starts running: with the main() method.

blocks.statement: A Java program can be written completely without a class.
blocks.explanation: That's not possible: in Java, all code must be inside a class. There is no code that "floats around freely".

blocks.robotComment: Every Java program needs exactly one starting line — this is it. 🚀
blocks.body: Every Java program needs a starting point — a place where execution begins. This starting point is one very specific method called main(). When you start a Java program, the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) automatically looks for this method.

code.caption: As soon as you start this program, the JVM finds the main() method and begins execution right there.

blocks.body: The line "public static void main(String[] args)" is called the method's signature. Each word has a fixed meaning: "public" makes the method callable from outside, "static" means it belongs to the class itself (you don't need an object to start it), "void" means the method doesn't return a value, "main" is the fixed name the JVM looks for, and "(String[] args)" is a place for text arguments at program start — the parentheses must be there even if you don't use them.

code.code:
public static void main(String[] args) {

}
code.caption: This exact line is what the JVM expects as a program's starting point.

blocks.question: What does the JVM look for to start a Java program?
options: A method called main() with the exact signature
The first line in the source code, regardless of what it says
The longest method in the entire program
blocks.explanation: The JVM specifically looks for a method called main() with the exact signature "public static void main(String[] args)" — only this one is recognized as the starting point.

blocks.robotComment: Even one wrong letter here and the JVM will not find your program. ⚠️
blocks.body: If the signature isn't exactly right — for example wrong capitalization like "Main" instead of "main", or a missing word — the JVM won't recognize the method as the starting point. The program then can't be started.

blocks.sentence: For the JVM to start a program, it looks for a method called ___.
blocks.explanation: The JVM always looks for exactly one method called "main" as the starting point of a Java program.

blocks.statement: In Java, the main() method must always read exactly "public static void main(String[] args)".
blocks.explanation: The JVM only recognizes this exact signature as the starting point. Any deviation means the program won't start as expected.

blocks.robotComment: Next up: what exactly counts as a 'statement' in Java. ➡️
blocks.body: Inside the main() method, you write your program's actual statements — they are executed step by step, in the order they appear. We'll take a closer look at exactly what a "statement" is in the next lesson.

blocks.question: What does the keyword "void" mean in the main() method?
options: The method doesn't return a value
The method is empty and does nothing
The method can't be called by the JVM
blocks.explanation: "void" means the method doesn't return a value after it runs — it simply executes statements.

blocks.robotComment: A semicolon is Java's way of saying 'done with this thought.' ✅
blocks.body: A Java program consists of many small statements. A statement is a single instruction to the computer — for example "print this text". Every statement ends with a semicolon ";".

code.code: System.out.println("Hello, Java!");
code.caption: This is a single statement. It ends with a semicolon — the character that tells Java "done".

blocks.robotComment: Forget this tiny character and the compiler gets confused fast. ⚠️
blocks.body: The semicolon works like a period at the end of a sentence: it tells the compiler "this statement is complete, the next one follows". If you forget the semicolon, the compiler doesn't understand where a statement ends and reports an error.

code.caption: Here are two statements in a row. Java executes the first one first, then the second — in exactly that order.

blocks.statement: Every statement in Java must end with a semicolon.
blocks.explanation: A semicolon marks the end of every single statement in Java. Without this character, the compiler doesn't understand where the statement ends.

blocks.robotComment: No shortcuts yet — Java just runs your code top to bottom. ➡️
blocks.body: At its core, a Java program is nothing more than a sequence of such statements. The JVM processes them strictly in order — from top to bottom, one after another. At this point there are no "shortcuts" or jumps yet — it's purely step-by-step execution.

blocks.question: Which character marks the end of a statement in Java?
blocks.explanation: A semicolon (;) marks the end of every statement in Java.

blocks.body: Statements don't just float around freely — they always sit inside a block enclosed by curly braces { }, for example the block of the main() method. We'll see exactly how these blocks work in the next lesson.

blocks.sentence: Java executes a program's statements in order, from ___ to bottom.
blocks.explanation: Java processes statements strictly in the order they appear in the code — from top to bottom.

blocks.robotComment: Curly braces are how Java knows where a group of code starts and ends. 🧱
blocks.body: Curly braces { } group multiple statements together into a shared block in Java. A block marks a clear beginning and a clear end — for example the body of a class or the body of a method.

code.caption: The outer curly braces belong to the class "Main", the inner ones to the main() method.

blocks.robotComment: See how one block can live neatly inside another. 📦
blocks.body: Blocks can be nested inside one another, similar to a box inside another box. The block of the main() method lies completely inside the block of the class — it starts later and ends earlier than the class block.

code.caption: Marked with comments, you can clearly see: the method block lies entirely within the class block.

blocks.question: What are curly braces { } used for in Java?
options: To group related statements into a block
blocks.explanation: Curly braces { } group statements into a block, for example the body of a class or a method.

blocks.robotComment: Miss a closing brace and the compiler will let you know. ⚠️
blocks.body: Every opening brace { must eventually have a matching closing brace }. If one is missing, the compiler can't tell where a block ends and reports an error — even if the rest of the code is correct.

blocks.statement: Every opening curly brace { needs a matching closing brace }.
blocks.explanation: In Java, braces must always come in pairs. If a closing brace is missing, the code can't be compiled.

blocks.body: As a reminder: the class itself is a block, the main() method is another block inside it, and the individual statements from the last lesson sit inside these blocks. That's how everything in a Java program fits together.

blocks.sentence: The block of the main() method lies ___ the block of the class.
blocks.explanation: The method block is nested inside the class block — it lies completely within it.

blocks.statement: You can omit curly braces { } if the code is short enough.
blocks.explanation: Curly braces are mandatory for class and method blocks in Java — regardless of how short the code is.

blocks.robotComment: Time to pull together everything you have learned about the rules. 📋
blocks.body: You now know about classes, the main() method, statements, and code blocks. Now let's summarize a few basic syntax rules that apply to every Java program.

code.code:
System.out.println("Hello!"); // correct
system.out.println("Hello!"); // Error! Java is case-sensitive
code.caption: Java is "case-sensitive" — capitalization makes a difference. "System" and "system" are two completely different words as far as Java is concerned.

blocks.robotComment: Case matters everywhere in Java — no exceptions. 🔠
blocks.body: This applies to everything in Java: class names, method names, keywords like "class" or "public". A single letter with the wrong capitalization leads to a compiler error.
Another fixed rule: the name of the Java file must exactly match the name of the public class inside it, including capitalization, plus the ".java" extension.

code.caption: This class is called "Main", so the file must be named exactly "Main.java" — not "main.java" and not "MainClass.java".

blocks.statement: Java is case-sensitive (for example, "Main" and "main" are different).
blocks.explanation: Java is case-sensitive: capitalization matters everywhere, including class names and method names.

blocks.body: Indentation — meaning spaces at the start of a line that visually shift nested blocks inward — is, on the other hand, not necessary for the compiler. Java compiles code without any indentation just fine. Still, you should always indent cleanly, because it makes your code much easier for people to read.

code.caption: This code compiles just fine — it's simply much harder to read without indentation than the indented version above.

blocks.question: Which statement about indentation in Java is correct?
options: It is not necessary for the compiler, but it makes the code more readable
The compiler requires exactly four spaces of indentation
Without indentation, the code won't compile
Indentation replaces the semicolon at the end of a statement
blocks.explanation: Indentation only serves human readability. The Java compiler doesn't require it — semicolons and curly braces are the actual rules.

blocks.robotComment: You now have the complete rulebook for any Java program. 📖
blocks.body: In summary, every Java program follows these rules: the code lives in a class, execution starts in the main() method, every statement ends with a semicolon, related statements sit in a block of curly braces, Java is case-sensitive, and the file name must match the public class.

blocks.sentence: A file containing the class "public class Main" must be named ___.
blocks.explanation: The file name must exactly match the name of the public class, including capitalization, plus the ".java" extension.

questions.question: What best describes a class in Java?
options: A container or blueprint that holds your code together
A single number in the program
A comment that the compiler ignores
An error message from the compiler

questions.statement: A Java program can be written completely without a class.

questions.sentence: A Java program begins its execution in the ___ method.

questions.question: Which keyword in the main() signature means the method doesn't return a value?

questions.statement: A statement in Java must always end with a semicolon.

questions.sentence: Java executes a program's statements ___ (from top to bottom).
Curly braces { } group statements into a ___.

questions.statement: Every opening curly brace { needs a matching closing brace }.

questions.question: What must the file containing a class "public class Main" be named?

questions.statement: Java is case-sensitive.

blocks.robotComment: Time to make Java actually say something out loud. 🔊
blocks.body: To display anything on the screen (the "console") in Java, you need the command System.out.println(). It outputs the text that you pass to it in parentheses and quotation marks.

code.caption: This complete program outputs exactly one line: Hello, World!

blocks.robotComment: That little "ln" is doing more work than you would guess. 📏
blocks.body: The "ln" in println stands for "line". After the output, the cursor automatically jumps to a new line. So the next text begins below it, not right after it.

code.caption: Two println() calls produce two separate lines.

blocks.sentence: System.out.println() outputs text and then automatically jumps to a new ___.
blocks.explanation: The "ln" in println stands for "line". After the output, the next output automatically begins on a new line.

blocks.body: System.out is the destination of the output (the console). println is the method name. The text in parentheses and in double quotation marks is called a "String" — exactly what gets printed.

code.caption: You can write as many println() lines in a row as you like — each one produces its own line.

blocks.question: What happens after System.out.println("Hi"); outputs the text?
options: The cursor automatically jumps to a new line
The next text is appended directly after it, without a line break
blocks.explanation: println() automatically inserts a line break after the output — the next output begins on a new line.

blocks.robotComment: Miss the quotation marks here and Java gets very confused. ⚠️
blocks.body: Important: The text that println() should output must be in double quotation marks, for example "Hello". Without quotation marks, Java would interpret the text as program code rather than plain text.

blocks.statement: System.out.println() outputs text without any line break, just like System.out.print().
blocks.explanation: That is not true: println() automatically adds a line break after the output. print(), on the other hand, does not — that is exactly what distinguishes the two commands.

blocks.robotComment: print() is println()'s more low-key sibling — no automatic new line. 🔇
blocks.body: Besides println(), there is also System.out.print(). It works almost the same way, but with one important difference: print() does NOT jump to a new line at the end.

code.caption: Both texts end up right next to each other on the same line — with no space and no line break in between.

blocks.robotComment: The cursor just... stays put. That is the whole trick. 📍
blocks.body: That is the key difference from println(): after print(), the cursor stays exactly where the text ends. The next output is appended directly after it.

code.caption: "A" is printed without a line break, immediately followed by "B" via println() — which only then produces the line break. "C" therefore begins on a new line.

blocks.question: What does this code output?
options: "XY" on one line, then "Z" on a new line
"X" on one line, then "Y" and "Z" together on the next line
"X", "Y", and "Z" each on three separate lines
blocks.explanation: print("X") does not add a line break, so "Y" is appended directly: "XY". println("Y") then inserts a line break, so "Z" begins on a new line.

blocks.body: print() is handy when you want to build up an output piece by piece from multiple commands, but have it look like a single line at the end. Remember: you have to add spaces yourself — print() does not do that automatically.

code.caption: The spaces here are deliberately placed at the end of "Java " and "is " — otherwise the words would run together.

blocks.sentence: System.out.print() outputs text, but does not add a ___ afterward.
blocks.explanation: That is exactly the difference from println(): print() outputs the text but without then jumping to a new line.

blocks.statement: After System.out.print("Hi"); the next output automatically begins on a new line.
blocks.explanation: False — print() does not produce a line break. The next output is appended directly after "Hi", on the same line.

blocks.question: What is the main difference between System.out.print() and System.out.println()?
options: println() jumps to a new line after the output, print() does not
print() cannot output numbers, but println() can
println() is only meant for testing programs
There is no difference, both behave identically
blocks.explanation: println() automatically adds a line break at the end, while print() leaves the cursor on the same line. That is the only difference, but it is an important one.

blocks.robotComment: Some characters need a little help to show up in your text. 🔡
blocks.body: Sometimes you want to output things in a text that cannot simply be written as-is — for example a line break in the middle of a sentence, or a quotation mark. For this, there are "escape characters": a backslash (\) followed by a letter that has a special meaning.

code.caption: \n produces a line break — in the middle of a single println() call.

blocks.sentence: The escape character ___ produces a line break in the middle of the text.
blocks.explanation: \n stands for "newline" and produces a line break, even if the text is in just a single println() call.

blocks.body: The escape character \t produces a tab — a larger, even amount of spacing. This lets you roughly align text into columns.

code.caption: \t makes sure that "Max" and "17" line up roughly underneath each other, even though "Name:" and "Age:" have different lengths.

blocks.question: What is the escape character \t used for?
blocks.explanation: \t inserts a tab, i.e. a larger, even amount of spacing. This helps align text into columns.

blocks.robotComment: This trick lets a quotation mark exist peacefully inside a string. 💬
blocks.body: If you want to output a regular quotation mark in the middle of a text, there is a problem: Java would think the string ends there. The solution is \" — an "escaped" quotation mark that is treated as plain text.

code.caption: Without the backslash before the quotation marks, Java would end the string too early and report an error.

blocks.statement: To output a quotation mark inside a text, you write \" instead of just ".
blocks.explanation: Exactly — a plain " would end the string prematurely. With \", the quotation mark is treated as regular text.

blocks.robotComment: Even backslashes need their own special trick to print. ⚙️
blocks.body: And what if you want to output a backslash itself — for example in a file path? Since a single backslash normally starts an escape character, you have to double it: \\.

code.caption: Each \\ in the code produces exactly one single backslash in the output.

blocks.sentence: To output a single backslash, you write ___ in the code.
blocks.explanation: A backslash must be doubled (\\) so that Java understands it as "one real backslash" rather than the start of another escape character.

blocks.robotComment: You've basically got Java's whole output toolkit now — let's put it all together. 🧰
blocks.body: Now you will combine everything you have learned so far — println(), print(), and the escape characters \n, \t, and \" — to format output exactly the way you want it.

code.caption: Four println() calls produce four lines — a simple, clear list.

blocks.robotComment: One \n can replace four separate println() calls. ⚡
blocks.body: The same output can also be produced with just a single println() call if you use \n to separate the lines within the text.

code.caption: A single call with \n produces exactly the same output as four separate println() calls.

blocks.statement: System.out.println("A\nB"); produces the same output as two separate calls, System.out.println("A"); and System.out.println("B");.
blocks.explanation: \n produces a line break in the middle of the text — that is why the output looks exactly as if you had used two separate println() calls.

blocks.body: With \t you can make multiple lines look like a small table by aligning text into columns.

code.caption: Each line begins with a word followed by \t — this makes the prices line up roughly in a column.

blocks.question: Why do you use \t in multiple consecutive println() lines?
options: To align the text into columns, like in a small table
To make the program run faster
blocks.explanation: \t inserts a tab. When you use it at the same spot in multiple lines, the following words roughly line up into columns.

blocks.robotComment: Combining print() and println() lets you build a line piece by piece. 🧩
blocks.body: You can also combine print() and println() to build a line out of multiple parts — for example a label, immediately followed by a quote in quotation marks.

code.caption: print() keeps the cursor on the same line, println() then closes it off. \" produces the actual quotation marks in the quote.

blocks.sentence: In the example above, ___ is used so that "Quote: " and the quote appear on the same line.
blocks.explanation: print() outputs text without starting a new line afterward — that is why the quote is appended directly after "Quote: ".

blocks.question: What does this code output?

code.code:
System.out.print("Result:\t");
System.out.println("42");

options: One line: "Result:" followed by a tab and "42"
An error, because print() and println() cannot be combined
blocks.explanation: print() does not add a line break, so "42" stays on the same line as "Result:". \t adds a tab space before it.

questions.question: What happens automatically after System.out.println("Hi"); outputs the text?
options: The cursor jumps to a new line

questions.statement: System.out.print() automatically adds a line break at the end.

questions.sentence: The escape character ___ produces a line break in the middle of the text.

questions.question: What does this code output?

code.code:
System.out.print("A ");
System.out.println("test");

questions.statement: \t produces a tab that helps align text into columns.

questions.sentence: To output a quotation mark directly in the text, you write ___.

questions.question: Why do you have to write \\ to output a single backslash?
options: Because a single backslash is interpreted by Java as the start of an escape character
Because Java does not allow backslashes at all
Because a single backslash ends the program

questions.statement: System.out.println("A\nB"); produces the same output as two separate println() calls for "A" and "B".

questions.question: What does this code output?

code.code:
System.out.println("X");
System.out.println("Y");

options: "X Y" with a space in between

questions.sentence: With System.out.___(), the cursor stays on the same line after the output.

blocks.robotComment: Comments won't run, but they might just save future-you a headache. 📝
blocks.body: A comment is a note in the code that the Java compiler completely ignores. Comments never change what a program does — they exist purely for humans who read the code: yourself a few weeks from now, or colleagues who look at your code later.

code.caption: The compiler skips the line with the comment entirely — it has no effect whatsoever on the program.

blocks.statement: Comments are executed by the Java compiler like normal code.
blocks.explanation: Comments are completely ignored by the compiler. They have no effect whatsoever on what the program does.

blocks.robotComment: A comment that just repeats the code isn't pulling its weight. 📝
blocks.body: Code you write today, you often don't read again until weeks or months later — and by then you've forgotten why you wrote certain lines the way you did. A good comment immediately explains to you (or someone else) what's going on, without you having to think through the entire code again.

code.code:
// TODO: Add an evening greeting later
System.out.println("Good morning!");
code.caption: A TODO comment is a reminder to yourself or your team about what still needs to be done later.

blocks.sentence: A comment that marks an open task for later often begins with the word ___.
blocks.explanation: TODO comments are a widely used convention for marking open tasks directly in the code.

blocks.robotComment: This WHY vs WHAT distinction is the whole secret to good comments. 💡
blocks.body: Comments are especially valuable when they explain WHY something is done in the code — not just WHAT is done. The "what" can often be read directly from the code. The "why," on the other hand, exists only in the mind of the person who wrote the code.

code.caption: This comment explains the intent behind the code — information you can't tell from the code alone.

blocks.question: What are comments in Java mainly intended for?
options: For humans who need to read and understand the code
For the compiler, to avoid errors
To make the program run faster
blocks.explanation: Comments are aimed at humans. The compiler ignores them completely — they make the program neither faster nor slower.

blocks.robotComment: Two slashes and you're commenting — Java's simplest kind of note. ✏️
blocks.body: The simplest way to write a comment in Java is with two forward slashes: //. Everything on the same line after // is completely ignored by the compiler.

code.caption: The line with // is ignored. The line with System.out.println runs completely normally.

blocks.body: A single-line comment doesn't have to be on its own line. It can also appear directly after code on the same line — this is called an "inline comment."

code.code: System.out.println("Hello!"); // prints "Hello!" to the screen
code.caption: Java executes the code before the // and simply ignores the rest of the line after it.

blocks.sentence: A single-line comment in Java begins with the characters ___.
blocks.explanation: Two forward slashes (//) start a single-line comment in Java.

blocks.robotComment: Turning off code without deleting it is a handy trick. 🔌
blocks.body: With //, you can also temporarily "turn off" an entire line of code without deleting it. This is called "commenting out." Java then treats the line as if it weren't there at all.

code.caption: "Line 2" is never printed because the line is commented out. Only "Line 1" and "Line 3" appear.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.explanation: The middle line is commented out and therefore skipped. Only "A" and "C" are printed.

blocks.robotComment: One small catch about how far a // comment actually reaches. 👀
blocks.body: Important: // only comments out text up to the end of the current line. A line break automatically ends the comment — the next line is read as normal code again.

blocks.statement: The // comment automatically also applies to the next line of code.
blocks.explanation: A // comment automatically ends at the end of the line. The next line is treated as normal code again.

blocks.robotComment: Sometimes one line just is not enough room to explain yourself. 📄
blocks.body: Sometimes a single line isn't enough to explain something. For longer comments, Java has a second notation: the multi-line comment. It begins with /* and ends with */ — everything in between is ignored, no matter how many lines it spans.

code.caption: Everything between /* and */ is ignored by the compiler — even across multiple lines.

blocks.robotComment: This style is perfect for describing a whole file right at the top. 🗂️
blocks.body: Multi-line comments are especially well-suited for longer explanations — for example, to describe at the beginning of a file what a program actually does.

code.caption: The asterisks (*) at the start of each line are just a visual convention used by many Java programmers. For the compiler, all that matters is that everything is between /* and */.

blocks.sentence: A multi-line comment in Java begins with /* and ends with ___.
blocks.explanation: A multi-line comment is opened with /* and must be closed again with */.

blocks.body: Another practical use: with /* */ you can "turn off" multiple lines of code at once, without having to write // in front of every single line.

code.caption: Both "Middle" lines are completely skipped — only "Start" and "End" are printed.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.explanation: The block between /* and */ is completely ignored. Only "Start" and "End" are actually printed.

blocks.robotComment: Forgetting to close this one causes a very confusing kind of bug. ⚠️
blocks.body: An important difference from //: a multi-line comment always has to be closed with */. If you forget the */, the compiler treats all the remaining code up to the next */ as a comment — which can lead to confusing errors.

blocks.statement: A multi-line comment /* ... */ can span multiple lines.
blocks.explanation: That's exactly the advantage of /* */ over //: the comment can span any number of lines until it is closed with */.

blocks.robotComment: You know the syntax — now for writing GOOD comments. ✍️
blocks.body: You now know both types of comments in Java: // and /* */. But just as important as the syntax is knowing when and how to use comments effectively. Here are the most important rules for good comments.

Rule 1: Explain the WHY, not the WHAT. Good code is often already self-explanatory — what it does is visible from the code itself. A comment is usually only helpful when it explains the reason behind a decision.

code.caption: Both comments sit above the same line of code — but only the second one provides information the code alone doesn't show.

blocks.statement: The comment "// prints Hello" above System.out.println("Hello"); is an example of a good comment.
blocks.explanation: The comment merely repeats what the code already shows clearly. A good comment would instead explain why this line exists.

blocks.robotComment: A comment that lies is worse than no comment at all. ⚠️
blocks.body: Rule 2: Keep comments up to date. When the code changes but the comment doesn't, you end up with an outdated comment. An outdated comment is often worse than no comment at all — it misleads others (and yourself).

code.code:
// Prints the user's first name
System.out.println("Welcome back!");
code.caption: This comment was probably not updated after the code changed — it no longer describes what the line actually does.

blocks.sentence: A comment that no longer matches the current code is called ___.
blocks.explanation: A comment that no longer matches the changed code is outdated — and can be misleading.

blocks.robotComment: Comment overload can actually make code harder to read. 🌀
blocks.body: Rule 3: Don't over-comment. If every single, obvious line gets its own comment, the code becomes more cluttered instead of clearer. Use comments purposefully: to mark sections or to explain truly tricky parts.

code.caption: Comments should appear where they truly provide guidance — not on every simple line.

blocks.question: When is a comment most useful?
options: When it explains why something is done, or usefully marks a section
When it appears before every single line of code
When it simply repeats what the code already shows
When it is as long as possible
blocks.explanation: Comments are most valuable when they provide context or reasons that aren't obvious from the code itself — not when they merely repeat the code.

questions.question: What are comments in Java mainly used for?
options: To make code more understandable for humans
To make the program run faster

questions.statement: The Java compiler executes the text in a comment like normal code.

questions.sentence: A single-line comment in Java begins with the characters ___.

questions.question: What happens to the code after // on the same line?
options: It is ignored by the compiler

questions.statement: A single-line comment with // automatically also applies to the next line.

questions.sentence: A multi-line comment begins with /* and ends with ___.

questions.question: What is a multi-line comment (/* ... */) especially well-suited for?
options: Longer explanations, or turning off multiple lines of code at once

questions.statement: With /* */, you can comment out multiple lines of code at once.

questions.question: What is an example of a good comment?
options: A comment that explains why a line of code exists
A comment that simply repeats the code
A comment on every single line

questions.statement: An outdated comment that no longer matches the code can do more harm than good.

blocks.robotComment: Variables are how your program remembers things — let's give data a name. 📦
blocks.body: A variable is a named container that stores a piece of data your program can work with and change while it runs. In Java, every variable must have a declared type, so the compiler always knows what kind of data it is allowed to hold.

code.code:
int age = 25;
System.out.println(age);
code.caption: Declaring an int variable named age, giving it the value 25, and then printing it.

blocks.robotComment: Notice how this pattern reads almost like a sentence: type, name, value. 🔤
blocks.body: The general pattern for declaring and initializing a variable is: type name = value;. Here, int is the type, age is the name, and 25 is the value assigned with the = operator. You don't have to assign a value right away — you can declare a variable first and give it a value later, as long as you assign something before you try to use it.

blocks.robotComment: Naming rules feel picky at first, but they make code predictable. 📛
blocks.body: Variable names in Java must start with a letter, an underscore (_), or a dollar sign ($) — never a digit — and cannot be one of Java's reserved keywords (like class or int). Names are case-sensitive, so score and Score are two different variables. By convention, Java developers write variable names in camelCase: the first word is lowercase, and each following word starts with a capital letter, e.g. totalScore or firstName.

blocks.sentence: In Java, variable names conventionally use ___, where the first word is lowercase and every following word starts with a capital letter, such as totalScore.
blocks.explanation: Java's naming convention for variables (and methods) is camelCase — lowercase first word, capitalized following words, no underscores.

blocks.body: A variable can also be reassigned: given a new value after it was already initialized. The new value simply replaces the old one — the old value is gone. The new value must still be compatible with the variable's declared type, since Java is statically typed and never lets a variable suddenly hold a different kind of data.

code.caption: Reassigning a variable using its own current value is a very common pattern, for example when tracking a changing score or a countdown.

blocks.question: What happens when you reassign a variable that already has a value?
options: The old value is replaced by the new one
Java keeps both values at the same time
blocks.explanation: Reassigning overwrites the previous value — a variable can only hold one value at a time.

blocks.robotComment: Quick gut check on how reassignment actually works. 🤔
blocks.statement: Once you declare a variable's type, you must write that type again every time you assign it a new value.
blocks.explanation: You only specify the type once, at declaration. After that, you simply write variableName = newValue; without repeating the type.

blocks.robotComment: Eight little types carry almost all the data in Java. 🧮
blocks.body: Every variable in Java needs a type, and the eight built-in primitive types are the most basic kinds of data a variable can hold. Unlike types you will meet later (like String), primitives are not objects — they store a simple value directly, which makes them fast and memory-efficient.

code.caption: Four commonly used primitive types: a whole number, a decimal number, a true/false value, and a single character.

blocks.robotComment: Four everyday types, four different jobs. 🔡
blocks.body: int stores whole numbers (no decimal point) and is the default choice for counting things — it can hold values from roughly -2.1 billion to 2.1 billion. double stores decimal numbers and is the default choice for anything with a fractional part, like prices or measurements. boolean can only ever be true or false, which makes it perfect for yes/no conditions. char stores exactly one character, written in single quotes like 'A' — never double quotes.

blocks.sentence: To store a single character like 'A', you use the ___ type.
blocks.explanation: char stores exactly one character and uses single quotes, unlike String which uses double quotes and can hold many characters.

blocks.body: Java also has smaller and larger whole-number types for when int isn't the right fit: byte and short save memory for tiny numbers, while long is used for whole numbers bigger than int can hold — you mark a long literal with an L at the end. float is a smaller, less precise alternative to double, rarely used unless memory is tight.

code.code:
long population = 8_000_000_000L;
byte smallNumber = 120;
code.caption: long needs an L suffix for its literal value; byte is useful for very small numbers where saving memory matters.

blocks.robotComment: Local variables don't get the same free pass as fields — keep that in mind here. 🤔
blocks.body: Fields that belong to a class automatically get a default value if you don't initialize them — 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, and a null character for char. Local variables declared inside a method, however, do not get a default value: Java's compiler forces you to assign one before you can use the variable, which helps catch bugs early.

blocks.statement: A local variable declared inside a method automatically gets a default value, like 0, if you never initialize it.
blocks.explanation: Local variables have no default value in Java — the compiler reports an error if you try to use one before assigning it a value.

blocks.question: Which primitive type would you use to store whether a light switch is on or off?
blocks.explanation: boolean is designed exactly for two-state, true/false values like on/off.

questions.question: Which type would you use to store a value like 4.99?

questions.sentence: A long literal in Java must end with the letter ___.

questions.question: What happens when you reassign a variable that already holds a value?
options: The old value is replaced by the new one

blocks.robotComment: Strings look simple, but under the hood they work differently from int. 🧵
blocks.body: String is one of the most-used types in Java, but it works differently from the primitives you just learned: String is a reference type (a class from the java.lang package), not a primitive. A String variable doesn't store the text directly the way an int stores a number — it stores a reference to a String object living elsewhere in memory. In everyday code, though, you can create and use Strings almost as easily as primitives.

code.caption: The + operator concatenates (joins) strings together, and automatically converts numbers to text when needed.

blocks.robotComment: These three methods will show up again and again in your code. 🔧
blocks.body: String comes with many useful methods. length() returns how many characters are in the string. charAt(index) returns the single character at a given position, counting from 0. substring(start, end) returns a new string containing the characters from start up to (but not including) end.

code.code:
String word = "Java";
System.out.println(word.length());        // 4
System.out.println(word.charAt(0));       // J
System.out.println(word.substring(1, 3)); // av
code.caption: length(), charAt(), and substring() are some of the most frequently used String methods.

blocks.robotComment: Once created, a String's text is locked in for good. 🔒
blocks.body: Strings are immutable: once a String object is created, its contents can never change. Methods like substring() don't modify the original string — they return a brand-new String with the result, leaving the original untouched.

blocks.robotComment: This is one of Java's classic gotchas — read closely before you answer. 👀
blocks.body: Because String is a reference type, the == operator compares whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory — not whether their text content is equal. To correctly check if two Strings contain the same characters, always use the .equals() method instead.

code.caption: a and b happen to be ==, but c is a separate object — only .equals() reliably compares String content.

blocks.sentence: To correctly compare the text content of two String objects, you should use the ___ method rather than the == operator.
blocks.explanation: == checks whether two variables reference the exact same object; .equals() checks whether their content is the same.

blocks.robotComment: Some values should just never change — final makes that a promise. 🔒
blocks.body: Sometimes a value should never change once it's set — think of the number of days in a week, or the maximum number of players allowed in a game. Java lets you mark a variable as a constant using the final keyword, which tells the compiler this variable's value must never change after it is assigned.

code.code:
final double PI = 3.14159;
System.out.println(PI);
code.caption: Declaring a constant with final — PI can be read, but never reassigned.

blocks.robotComment: ALL_CAPS names make constants impossible to miss in your code. 🔠
blocks.body: By convention, constant names are written in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: every letter capitalized, with underscores separating words, such as MAX_PLAYERS or DAYS_IN_WEEK. This makes constants instantly recognizable in your code, setting them apart at a glance from regular camelCase variables.

code.code:
final int MAX_PLAYERS = 4;
System.out.println(MAX_PLAYERS);
code.caption: MAX_PLAYERS follows the UPPER_SNAKE_CASE convention for constants.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly the kind of bug a good constant name prevents. 🎯
blocks.body: If you try to reassign a final variable after it has been given a value, the code will not compile — Java catches the mistake before the program ever runs. This is exactly why constants are so useful: they replace unexplained 'magic numbers' scattered through your code with a single, clearly named, protected value. If that value ever needs to change, you update it in exactly one place, and a name like MAX_PLAYERS makes the code's intent obvious to anyone reading it.

code.code:
final int MAX_LIVES = 3;
MAX_LIVES = 5; // Compile-time error: cannot assign a value to final variable MAX_LIVES
code.caption: The compiler stops you from ever changing a final variable's value.

blocks.sentence: The ___ keyword tells Java that a variable's value can never be changed after it is first assigned.
blocks.explanation: final marks a variable as a constant — any attempt to reassign it causes a compiler error.

blocks.question: What happens if you try to reassign a variable declared with final?
options: Nothing — final has no real effect
blocks.explanation: Reassigning a final variable is a compile-time error in Java.

blocks.statement: By convention, constant names in Java are written in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, like MAX_SPEED.
blocks.explanation: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants is a widely followed Java naming convention.

blocks.robotComment: Converting between types isn't always free — some directions are riskier. 🔄
blocks.body: Type casting means converting a value from one type to another. Java has two kinds: implicit (widening) casting, which happens automatically when no data can be lost, and explicit (narrowing) casting, which you must write yourself because it risks losing information.

code.caption: Widening happens automatically because every int value fits perfectly inside a double.

blocks.robotComment: Explicit casts are Java's way of making you own the risk. ✍️
blocks.body: Going the other way — from a larger or more precise type to a smaller one, like double to int — is called narrowing, and Java requires you to write an explicit cast: the target type in parentheses right before the value. This forces you to acknowledge that some information might be lost.

code.caption: Casting a double to int truncates (cuts off) the decimal part — it does not round.

blocks.robotComment: Overflow bugs are sneaky — the number doesn't error, it just lies. 🐛
blocks.body: Precision loss isn't limited to decimals: casting a whole-number type into a smaller one can also lose data if the value doesn't fit. When that happens, the number can "wrap around" into a completely unexpected — even negative — result, which is a common source of subtle bugs.

code.caption: Casting a value too large to fit into int causes it to overflow instead of simply being cut down.

blocks.sentence: Converting a larger type into a smaller one, such as double to int, is called ___ casting and requires an explicit cast.
blocks.explanation: Narrowing casting risks losing data, so Java requires you to explicitly request it with (targetType).

blocks.explanation: Casting a double to int simply cuts off the decimal part rather than rounding.

blocks.explanation: Widening never loses data, so Java performs it implicitly without requiring a cast.
